children: Himanshi Lohchab & Tanya Pandey Mumbai | New Delhi: The past six days' deluge of cyber incidents has shone a spotlight on gaps in India's data protection legislation. Artificial intelligence (AI) is testing what it means to keep personal data safe.

Can a company be held responsible when an attacker moves faster than a flaw can be patched? Can data processors be penalised when AI creates an overnight systemic risk to the internet? And who is accountable when an AI assistant goes rogue? As companies edge closer to the May 2027 enforcement deadline for the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) law, AI's emerging cybersecurity risks are creating tension over what might constitute adequate compliance just six to seven months from now.

On October 15, CERT-In warned that AI agents under testing had accessed the systems of Indian organisation without authorisation. It also flagged that attackers were using AI tools to syphon off funds. India's largest lender, State Bank of India, later disclosed a breach that leaked the personal data of 375,000 customers on the dark web.

Days later, two critical flaws in PHP, the software used to run websites, suddenly put 70% of the internet at risk of cyberattacks. For India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) framework, the challenge lies in defining what "reasonable security safeguards" should mean in such scenarios.

Experts suggest that an attack alone does not establish a compliance failure. However, what precautions should companies be expected to take? Furthermore, how should responsibility be shared when a business, an AI provider and a customer are all involved? What counts as reasonable protection? "The penalty attaches to inadequate safeguards, not to the breach itself," said Arun Prabhu, partner at law firm Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas.

A company attacked through a previously unknown vulnerability despite sound security practices should be treated differently from one running outdated or unpatched systems, according to him. "No organisation can ever guarantee absolute immunity from sophisticated cyberattacks, particularly where previously unknown vulnerabilities are exploited before effective patches become available," said Hardeep Sachdeva, senior partner at law firm AZB. The test should determine whether safeguards were reasonable, proportionate and demonstrable.

With potential penalties extending to 250 crore, companies require clarity on how regulators will assess their efforts. Sachdeva said that while patching, monitoring, independent assessments and documented response procedures should count as evidence of diligence, they should not automatically shield a company from liability. The problem often starts before a company can deploy a fix, as it may not know where vulnerable software is running, said Mini Gupta, partner, cybersecurity consulting, EY India.

title: Code Red, Law Dud? Rogue AI Agents Exposing India's Data Law Blindspots
